passages.title: Email Correspondence: Appealing a Course Withdrawal

emails.subject: Appeal — withdrawal from BIOL 240
emails.body:
Dear Registrar's Office,

I am writing to appeal my administrative withdrawal from BIOL 240, which I learned of yesterday when the course disappeared from my portal.

The withdrawal was applied because my tuition instalment was eleven days late. The payment was late because my student loan disbursement was delayed by the provincial office — I have attached their letter confirming the delay was on their side and not mine. The full amount was paid on November 9, before I was notified of any problem.

BIOL 240 is a prerequisite for two courses I am registered for in January. If the withdrawal stands, I lose a full year, because the course runs only in the autumn term. I have attended every laboratory session and my current standing is 82 per cent.

I would like the withdrawal reversed. If that is not possible administratively, I would be grateful to know what the formal appeal process involves and what the deadline is, since I do not want to miss a second deadline while waiting for a reply to this one.

With thanks,
Daniel Osei
Student number 4471902

emails.subject: RE: Appeal — withdrawal from BIOL 240
emails.body:
Dear Mr Osei,

Thank you for writing promptly and for attaching the letter from the provincial loan office — that document is what makes this straightforward.

Where a payment delay is documented as originating with a funding body rather than the student, our policy allows the withdrawal to be reversed administratively without a formal appeal. I have therefore reinstated your registration in BIOL 240 with effect from today, and your standing of 82 per cent is unaffected.

Two things to be aware of. Reinstatement restores the registration but does not automatically remove the late-payment notation from your account; I have submitted the request to have it cleared, which usually takes five working days. Please check your account after that and contact me directly if it is still showing.

Second, your January registrations were auto-cancelled when the prerequisite lapsed. Those do not restore themselves. You will need to re-register for both courses, and I would do that today rather than at the end of the week — both have waiting lists.

I am sorry this happened. The system applies withdrawals automatically at eleven days and does not check whether the delay was the student's fault, which is a problem we have raised internally.

Regards,
Helena Cruz
Associate Registrar

passages.title: Why Adults Learn Differently
passages.content:
Adult education has been shaped for decades by a claim that sounds obvious and turns out to be only partly true: that adults learn differently from children. The distinction is real, but not always where people expect to find it.

The most durable finding concerns motivation. Adults return to study with a purpose that predates the course — a promotion, a licence, a language they need for a new country. This is why adult learners tolerate difficulty that would defeat a teenager, and also why they abandon courses that seem irrelevant. A child asks whether the material will be examined; an adult asks what it is for. Programmes that cannot answer the second question lose their students by the third week.

Experience is the second difference, and it cuts both ways. An adult brings a store of knowledge that new material can be attached to, which is why a bookkeeper learns accounting software faster than a school-leaver. But experience also produces confident errors, and unlearning something is measurably harder than learning it for the first time. Instructors of adults spend more time dismantling than building.

The claim about a fixed decline in ability with age has been substantially revised. Processing speed does decline, and this is genuine — an older learner will generally take longer on unfamiliar material. Vocabulary, reasoning from context and pattern recognition do not decline in the same way, and often improve. The practical consequence is that adults do worse on tasks requiring rapid unfamiliar recall and no worse, sometimes better, on tasks that reward accumulated knowledge.

Where the popular account is least reliable is on so-called learning styles. The idea that a student is a visual, auditory or kinaesthetic learner, and should be taught accordingly, remains widely repeated and has not survived testing. Studies that match teaching method to a student's stated style consistently fail to find the predicted advantage. What does help is matching the method to the material: a procedure is best demonstrated, an argument best discussed, a vocabulary list best tested by retrieval.

The most useful practical finding is unglamorous. Retrieval practice — being made to recall something without looking — produces markedly better retention than re-reading, at every age. Most adult learners report that re-reading feels more effective, which is precisely why it persists.

passages.title: Should Universities Drop Standardised Admission Tests?

viewpoints.name: Prof. Alan Whitfield, admissions dean
viewpoints.text: We went test-optional for four years and I have changed my mind twice. What we found was not that tests are unfair but that dropping them shifted weight onto things that are more unfair — extracurriculars, essays that can be coached, references whose quality depends on how well-resourced your school is. A test score is a narrow measure, but it is a measure everyone sits under the same conditions. Removing it did not remove advantage; it moved it somewhere harder to see.

viewpoints.name: Rosa Delgado, secondary school counsellor
viewpoints.text: I work in a school where most students are the first in their family to apply anywhere. For them the test is a toll booth. The score correlates with preparation, and preparation correlates with money — my students cannot buy a twelve-week course. When we went test-optional our applications rose by a third and our acceptances rose with them. I am not claiming the test measures nothing. I am saying it measures something we have not distributed fairly.

viewpoints.name: Dr Yusuf Rahman, education researcher
viewpoints.text: Both of the above are describing real effects, which is why the evidence looks contradictory. Test scores do predict first-year performance, modestly, and they predict it better when combined with school grades than either does alone. They also under-predict for students from under-resourced schools, meaning those students outperform their scores. The sensible reading is not abolish or restore, but weight appropriately and interpret in context — which requires admissions staff and time, and is therefore the option institutions are least willing to fund.

viewpoints.name: Meera Pillai, current undergraduate
viewpoints.text: I applied in the first test-optional year and I still do not know whether that helped me. What I do know is that the uncertainty was its own burden. Nobody could tell us whether submitting a decent-but-not-brilliant score would help or hurt, so we all guessed. If institutions keep the tests, say so and say what a competitive score is. If they drop them, drop them properly. It is the ambiguity that punishes students who have nobody to ask.
